title: Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues
hook: Opens by naming the exact student anxieties ('Why are we doing this?' / 'What does this actually mean?') via animated pi-creature classroom, making the video feel like a direct response to a felt need.

scenes.purpose: Validate student confusion and reframe the real obstacle as missing prerequisites, not the topic itself

on_screen.desc: Title: Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues
Animated pi-creature classroom with confused/tired/sassy students
Student speech bubbles: 'Why are we doing this?' / 'What does this actually mean?'
det(A - λI) = 0 equation in teacher speech bubble

scenes.transition: Classroom scene fades; prerequisite grid appears
scenes.narration_gist: Students find eigenstuffs confusing not because the topic is hard, but because their foundation in prior concepts is shaky.

scenes.purpose: Name the four prerequisite concepts visually so the viewer knows what mental toolkit is needed

on_screen.desc: Header: Many prerequisites
2×2 grid of rectangles labeled: Linear transformations, Determinants, Linear systems, Change of basis

scenes.transition: Grid fades; grid plane and example transformation animate in
scenes.narration_gist: You need solid visual understanding of linear transformations, determinants, linear systems, and change of basis before eigenvectors click.

scenes.purpose: Show concretely what it means for a vector to stay on its own span under a transformation

on_screen.desc: Animated grid undergoing linear transformation with matrix [[3,0],[1,2]]
A vector and its span line (Maroon) before and after transform
Label: 'Vector gets knocked off Span' or 'Vector remains on its own span'
Matrix [[3,0],[1,2]] displayed top-left

scenes.transition: Same grid kept; new vectors highlighted to show eigenvector cases
scenes.narration_gist: Most vectors rotate off their span, but special eigenvectors only get stretched or squished, staying on the line they define.

scenes.purpose: Name eigenvectors and eigenvalues and show both eigenspaces of the example matrix

on_screen.desc: Full set of x-axis vectors (yellow) and diagonal-line vectors (maroon) displayed after transformation
Label: 'Eigenvectors — Stretched by 3' on x-axis
Label: 'Eigenvectors — Stretched by 2' on diagonal
Eigenvalue labels: 'with eigenvalue 3' and 'with eigenvalue 2'

scenes.transition: Eigenspace labels stay; scene cuts to 3D rotation teaser then returns to symbolic setup
scenes.narration_gist: These special vectors are eigenvectors; the scalar factor by which each is stretched is its eigenvalue.

scenes.purpose: Translate the geometric idea into the symbolic equation Av = λv and expose the core algebraic manipulation

on_screen.desc: Large equation: A·v = λ·v with A, v, λ labeled via braces
Brace label: 'Matrix-vector multiplication' under left side
Brace label: 'Scalar multiplication' under right side

scenes.transition: Braces fade; right side is rewritten as matrix multiplication
scenes.narration_gist: The eigenvector equation says matrix multiplication equals scalar multiplication; we need to reconcile the two types.

scenes.purpose: Derive the determinant condition by showing why (A − λI) must squish space

on_screen.desc: Equation chain: Av = λv → (A − λI)v = 0 → det(A − λI) = 0
Sample matrix with λ subtracted from diagonal entries
det(A − λI) = 0 enlarged and centered

scenes.transition: Equation highlighted and isolated; interactive λ-tweak animation loads
scenes.narration_gist: Rearranging forces det(A − λI) = 0 because a non-zero solution for v requires the transformation to squish space.

scenes.purpose: Make the determinant condition visceral by animating the grid collapsing as λ is tuned to the eigenvalue

on_screen.desc: Animated grid squishing as λ dial changes from 0 to 3
Matrix (A − λI) with live decimal λ values on diagonal
Determinant readout changing in real time, hitting 0 at sweet spot

scenes.transition: Grid restored; worked example for λ=2 and eigenvector computation shown
scenes.narration_gist: Tweaking λ until the determinant hits zero is the sweet spot — that λ is an eigenvalue and the collapsed space reveals the eigenvector.

scenes.purpose: Show edge cases: no real eigenvectors (90° rotation), repeated eigenvalue with a full plane of eigenvectors (scaling)

on_screen.desc: 90° rotation grid — every vector rotates off its span
Polynomial λ²+1=0, roots ±i (no real eigenvectors)
Uniform 2× scaling grid — every vector is an eigenvector
Shear matrix shown with only x-axis eigenvectors, λ=1 only root

scenes.narration_gist: Some transformations have no real eigenvectors; others have a full plane — both are illuminated by the determinant equation.

scenes.purpose: Introduce eigenbasis: show that using eigenvectors as basis vectors diagonalizes the matrix and makes repeated multiplication trivial

on_screen.desc: Grid shown in eigenvector coordinate system; transformation becomes diagonal
Change-of-basis sandwich: C⁻¹AC displayed as diagonal matrix with eigenvalues
Diagonal matrix [[−1,0],[0,2]] with eigenvalues highlighted on diagonal

scenes.transition: Morty character poses the 100th-power problem as a closing challenge
scenes.narration_gist: Changing to an eigenbasis turns the matrix diagonal, making operations like computing the 100th power straightforward.

scenes.purpose: Close with a practical puzzle prompt and tease the next topic

on_screen.desc: Puzzle prompt left on screen for viewer
Next video teaser: Abstract vector spaces

scenes.narration_gist: An optional puzzle lets viewers apply eigenbasis thinking; the series continues with abstract vector spaces.

lessons: Open by voicing the audience's own frustrations before explaining anything — it earns trust and frames the entire lesson.
Show the prerequisite map visually before diving in, so viewers can self-diagnose their own gaps instead of feeling globally lost.
Introduce a concept geometrically first, then name it, so the label arrives as a reward rather than a demand to memorize.
Use a real-time parameter animation (the λ dial) to let viewers see a continuous process rather than just before-and-after snapshots.
Place counter-examples (rotation with no eigenvectors, scaling with infinite eigenvectors) immediately after the main definition to stress-test and deepen understanding.
Reserve the most powerful payoff scene (eigenbasis diagonalization) for late in the arc, after the viewer has earned the intuition needed to appreciate it.
